title: Return a Whole Dispatch
content:
What problem does this solve?
return can send any Python value back to the caller, including a whole list or dictionary. That lets a function package several related results into one structure instead of only returning one number or string.

Return the structure you built
  def pair(a, b):
      return [a, b]
The caller receives one list containing both values.

Finish the work before return
  def labels(items):
      lines = []
      for item in items:
          lines.append(f"Item: {item}")
      return lines
If return were inside the loop, the function would stop after the first item.

Named results
  def summary(name, score):
      return {"name": name, "score": score}
A dictionary is useful when the labels are part of the meaning of the result.

Scope boundary for this lesson
We are learning what structure a function returns and where return belongs. Whether two variables share the same mutable object is deliberately saved for Lesson 24.

Vocabulary after the behavior
A structured return value is a list or dictionary returned as one result. The caller is the code that called the function and receives that result.
concepts: A function can return a list or dictionary
Building a collection is not enough; the function must return it
When collecting many items, return usually belongs after the loop
A dictionary can package several named results into one return value

examples.title: Return a list
examples.explanation: The caller receives one list containing both input values.

examples.title: Forgot to return
examples.explanation: The list was created, but the caller receives None because no return ran.

examples.title: Return after the loop
examples.explanation: Every item contributes before the finished list is returned.

examples.title: Return a dictionary
examples.code:
def summary(name, score):
    return {"name": name, "score": score}
examples.explanation: Named keys make the returned fields self-describing.

common_mistakes: Building a result collection and forgetting to return it
Printing the collection instead of returning it
Returning from inside a loop after only the first item
Choosing an unlabeled list when the caller needs named fields
Introducing copying/shared-reference rules before the reference model is taught

exercises.title: Built but not returned
hints: The function creates a list, but ask whether it ever sends that list back.
Reaching the end of a function without return gives the caller None.
print receives None, so it prints None.

exercises.title: Return two values as one list
exercises.prompt: Write `make_pair(a, b)` that returns exactly `[a, b]`.
hints: The returned value itself should be a list.
Build the list from the two parameter names, not fixed sample values.
Return `[a, b]`.

exercises.title: Return one record
exercises.prompt: Write `make_point(x, y)` that returns exactly `{"x": x, "y": y}`.
exercises.reference_solution:
def make_point(x, y):
    return {"x": x, "y": y}
hints: This result needs named fields, so use a dictionary.
The keys are the literal strings x and y; the values come from the parameters.
Return `{"x": x, "y": y}`.

exercises.title: Return stops the function
hints: Trace only the first loop pass before looking at the next item.
After a is appended, return runs immediately and the function ends.
The caller receives ['a']; b and c are never processed.

exercises.title: Return after the loop
exercises.prompt: The function returns after labeling only the first item. Move `return` so all items are processed. Do not change the string format.
hints: return ends the entire function, not only the current loop pass.
Let the loop finish building lines before the function sends the list back.
Dedent `return lines` so it is after the for loop.

exercises.title: Collect selected names
exercises.prompt: Write `long_names(names)` that returns a new list containing every name whose length is at least 5. Use a for loop, an if statement, len(), and append(). Do not return from inside the loop.
hints: Start with an empty result list and visit every input name.
Append a name only when `len(name) >= 5`.
Return the completed result after the loop, not from inside it.

exercises.title: Return a summary dictionary
exercises.prompt: Write `party_summary(party, supplies)` returning exactly two keys: `member_count` and `supply_count`, each calculated with len(). Do not print the result.
hints: The caller needs two named results, so return one dictionary.
Calculate each value from its corresponding parameter with len().
Return exactly the two required keys; do not hardcode counts from one example.

exercises.title: Expedition Dispatch System v1
exercises.prompt: Write `build_dispatch(destination, party, supplies, status="Review")`. Return a dictionary containing exactly `destination`, `member_count`, `supply_count`, and `status`. Calculate both counts with len(). Use the default status when omitted and accept an override. Do not print inside the function, and do not add copying/shared-reference behavior yet.
exercises.starter_code:
def build_dispatch(destination, party, supplies, status="Review"):
    pass
hints: Build one dictionary from the four pieces of information the caller needs.
destination and status come directly from parameters; both counts come from len() of the list parameters.
Return the dictionary once. Keep status defaulted to Review in the signature and let callers override it.
exercises.success_message: Dispatch packet complete. You combined richer function interfaces with structured returned data without crossing into reference/copy semantics early.
